title: Resistor Color Code Decoder
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Clocks and Watches with AI
description: Click the bands of a large four-band resistor to change their colors and read its value, then quiz yourself by reading random resistors or setting the bands to match a value.

educational.topic: Reading the four-band resistor color code
learningObjectives: Recall the digit value of each resistor band color.
Apply the color code to read the value of a four-band resistor.
Apply the color code in reverse to choose the bands for a given value.
prerequisites: Read the Resistors section of Chapter 2.
Know that 1 kΩ = 1,000 Ω and 1 MΩ = 1,000,000 Ω.

accessibility.notes: Screen-reader description provided; all controls are standard HTML elements.

controls.label: Resistor bands
controls.description: Cycles the color of the clicked band (not used in the read-the-bands quiz).

controls.label: Mode
controls.description: Chooses free exploration or one of the two quizzes.

controls.label: Random resistor
controls.description: Shows a random resistor (Explore and read quiz) or a random target value (set quiz).

controls.label: Your value
controls.description: The value you read, or the value you want the bands to make.

controls.label: Check
controls.description: Checks the answer and updates the score.

keyQuestions: Why is the first band never black?
What does the third band tell you?
What colors would a 10 kΩ ±5% resistor have?
commonMisconceptions: Reading the multiplier band as a third digit (reading red as "2" instead of "×100").
Reading the resistor from the wrong end. The tolerance band (gold or silver) goes on the right.
Thinking tolerance changes the value. It only says how far the real value may be from the marked value.
assessmentOpportunities: Students score at least 8 out of 10 when reading random resistors.
Students can name the four bands for a given value such as 4.7 kΩ ±5% (yellow-violet-red-gold).
Students explain what the tolerance band means for a real 330 Ω ±5% resistor (between about 314 Ω and 347 Ω).
